why_go: January is peak birding at Chidiya Tapu. Temperatures hold steady at 23-29°C, and the morning trails are dry. Migratory species arrive in full strength during this window, concentrating at remaining mangrove waterholes.
February is the driest month, with crisp dawn birding conditions and calm sea. Mangrove walks remain completely dry. Post-Valentine weekdays offer relief from December-January crowds.
Late-season peak. March trails remain dry and sunset viewpoints are clear. Hotel rates in Port Blair drop 25 percent, making this an economical choice for the full birding window.
April offers hot-but-dry conditions at 27-33°C. Trails stay passable through the month. Quiet weekday afternoons deliver near-solitude, and off-peak pricing remains available in Port Blair.
Early May provides the last clean trekking window before monsoon. Trails are safe through May 20. Morning birding remains productive, though peak humidity begins reducing visibility by month-end.
why_not: Peak humidity reduces bird visibility, the main draw here.
June brings Southwest monsoon swells of 420mm rain. NH-223 floods and trails become leech-thick. Sunset point becomes unusable, and most migratory birds have departed for cooler ground.
July is peak monsoon with 480mm rainfall and road washouts on NH-223. Forest Department sometimes closes trails entirely during this month. Conditions remain treacherous throughout.
August monsoon continues with 410mm rain and muddy trails. Sunset point remains clouded. Wildlife is dispersed, making this month unrewarding for the primary birding goal.

why_go: Late-monsoon trails begin reopening in the final week. Road becomes usable from mid-month onward. Rainfall drops to 270mm as monsoon retreats.
why_not: Trails remain waterlogged despite monsoon retreat, making hiking treacherous. Migratory birds haven't begun returning in force yet.

why_go: Season reopens in October. Trails dry by mid-month and rainfall settles at 130mm, mostly in the first week. Sunset clears and migrant arrivals accelerate through the month.
why_not: Post-monsoon rains remain frequent in early October. Bird migrations haven't fully peaked, making early-month visits less rewarding than late-month.

why_go: November is a strong shoulder month with only 60mm rain. Migrants are returning in force and trails remain dry. Diwali week brings crowds, but weekdays stay peaceful.
December is peak season. Sea stays calm, trails are bone-dry, and bird populations reach full strength. Christmas-New Year week sees packed sunset point, but wildlife activity is at year-maximum.
January is peak coffee season at Chikmagalur. Mullayanagiri (1,930m) is clearest, and plantation walks deliver year-best conditions at 12-26°C. The mountain air carries the scent of fresh coffee.
February is the driest month. Mullayanagiri reaches its clearest views of the year. Plantation walks are impeccable. Coffee harvest tail continues, and the elevation keeps temperatures pleasant.
March opens the Coffee Blossom window. White-flower carpets blanket plantations 7-10 days after pre-monsoon showers. Temperatures at 15-30°C remain manageable. This is the most aromatic month.
why_not: Pre-monsoon heat and scattered showers make hiking uncomfortable despite the elevation's mitigating coolness.

why_go: April catches the Coffee Blossom tail. Mullayanagiri remains climbable early in the month. Temperatures rise to 17-32°C, but pre-monsoon thunderstorms only intensify in the final 10 days.
why_not: Daytime temperatures peak above 35°C, making trails unbearably hot in April's second half.

why_go: May brings pre-monsoon storms, but the first half remains trekable if you start early. Temperatures at 18-31°C are manageable at elevation. SW monsoon advance squalls only dominate the final 10 days.
why_not: Peak heat and sticky humidity make hiking the coffee plantations uncomfortable. Visibility collapses by late month, reducing the appeal.

why_go: June brings SW monsoon onset with 600-800mm rainfall, but the elevation and plantations offer respite from lowland humidity. Mullayanagiri road closes intermittently, but early-month access may be possible.
why_not: Leeches infest all trails during peak monsoon season. Landslide risk on NH-73 makes travel unpredictable.
July is peak monsoon with 800-1,100mm rainfall. NH-73 is landslide-prone and summit roads close. The combination of heavy rain and unstable slopes makes this month genuinely unsafe.

why_go: August monsoon continues, but NH-73 stabilises as rainfall eases to 600-800mm. Hebbe Falls reaches peak flow. The green is at its most saturated, and plantation canopy offers shelter.
why_not: Monsoon rains trigger frequent landslides on mountain roads through August. Travel risk remains elevated.

why_go: September marks monsoon retreat. Rainfall drops to 300-500mm. Mullayanagiri reopens. Plantations are at their greenest year-round, and the cooler air returns.
October opens the full season. NE monsoon residual keeps plantations lush at 14-26°C. Hebbe Falls maintains strong flow. The landscape is photogenic in its fullest green.
High season builds. Coffee Arabica harvest begins. Mullayanagiri is crystal-clear and dry at 13-26°C. Plantations are at their most photogenic, combining harvest activity with peak season clarity.
December is peak season. Coffee Robusta and Arabica harvests overlap. Mullayanagiri offers year-best clarity. Temperatures drop to 11-24°C, making all-day trekking comfortable.
January recovery from rare rains. 14-28°C is ideal for the Thoovanam Falls trek, which is bone-dry. Grizzled Giant Squirrel sightings climb. Permits are straightforward from Marayoor.

February is the driest month and sharpest for visibility. Trail conditions are at year-firmest. Wildlife concentrates at remaining waterholes, making sightings more probable. This is prime sanctuary season.
March heat reaches 22-34°C in the rain-shadow. Trails are workable at dawn and dusk. Wildlife concentrates intensely at waterholes, offering rare viewing opportunities.
why_not: Bone-dry conditions concentrate wildlife at waterholes, but midday heat makes trekking genuinely punishing. Daytime sightseeing is reduced to early-morning windows.
Peak rain-shadow heat hits 26-37°C. Trails become dangerous past 9am. Falls reduce to trickles. The extreme heat and dry season make both trekking and wildlife spotting futile.
Rain-shadow heat continues at 28-38°C. Falls are dry and trails are unsafe. Peak heat and humidity combine to make wildlife spotting poorest of the year.

why_go: SW monsoon brings only 100-150mm rainfall in the rain-shadow, leaving trails workable but humidity elevated. Heat residual makes conditions marginal.
why_not: Monsoon rains make trails impassable and wildlife spotting nearly impossible. The rain-shadow receives less water, but enough to disrupt trekking.
Rain-shadow monsoon brings 150-200mm rainfall. Wildlife disperses. NH-85 approach becomes unreliable. The combination of rains and dispersed wildlife makes July unrewarding.
Rain-shadow monsoon continues at 100-150mm rainfall. Wildlife remains dispersed. Onam festival closures affect Marayoor access. August offers poor conditions across all metrics.

why_go: Rain-shadow recovery begins. Rainfall eases to 80-120mm. Falls begin flowing again. NH-85 stabilises. Wildlife begins congregating as the monsoon fully retreats.
why_not: September rain-shadow monsoon peaks with 80-120mm rainfall. Trails remain muddy and wildlife spotting remains nearly impossible.

why_go: NE monsoon hits the TN border, bringing 200-300mm rainfall and strong falls flow. 22-30°C is ideal. Wildlife concentration begins to return.
why_not: Thoovanam Falls peaks in October but trails remain slick from monsoon runoff. Sighting probability is high, but terrain is slippery.

why_go: November opens peak Chinnar season. 18-28°C is ideal. NE monsoon has spent itself, falls flow strong, and trails dry completely. Wildlife concentration intensifies as the season deepens.
December peak season continues. 16-28°C with building wildlife concentration. Falls maintain strong flow. Christmas-New Year rates climb at Munnar, but Marayoor stays calm and accessible.
January is the peak fort-trek window. 16-29°C is perfect climbing weather. The seven concentric walls and Obavva cleft walks are at year-cleanest. Granite photography is sharp.
February is the driest month. 18-32°C holds steady. Fort photography delivers year-best granite-and-sky contrast. Obavva cleft walks are bone-dry and unobstructed.
March is the last cool month at 20-35°C. Fort climbing compresses to before 10am as granite radiates heat at midday. Hotel rates drop 25 percent, making it economical.

why_not: April heat dome reaches 23-40°C. Granite boulder surfaces hit 48°C. The fort becomes physically closed by physics at midday. April is genuinely unsafe for climbing.
May heat peaks at 24-42°C with granite at 50°C plus. Pre-monsoon dust fouls views. The fort is closed, and conditions are extremely hostile.

why_go: SW monsoon brings 70-100mm rainfall and heat drops to 23-34°C. Walks are viable in morning and evening. This is a marginal window for those who accept cloudy skies.
why_not: Monsoon clouds obscure the fort's architecture and viewpoints for most of June. Photography suffers and the fort's scale is lost.

why_go: SW monsoon active at 22-30°C brings 90-120mm rainfall. Granite becomes slick, but walks remain viable in morning and evening. The boulder field drips with moisture.
why_not: Monsoon clouds obscure fort views and muddy trekking paths. Safety risk increases on slippery surfaces.

why_go: Monsoon continues at 21-29°C with 90-120mm rainfall. Boulder field turns green-mossed. Walks are viable in cool morning and evening hours.
why_not: Monsoon mud makes the fort's lower circuits safer than scrambling the slick upper walls. Risk of slips increases significantly.

why_go: Monsoon retreats at 20-28°C. Rainfall eases to 70-100mm. Green-moss boulder field is at peak beauty. This is the last off-peak window with acceptable conditions.
why_not: Monsoon rains make fort exploration wet and slippery despite moderate difficulty. Early-month conditions are worse than late-month.

why_go: Season reopens. 19-29°C with 30-50mm residual rain. Green-mossed boulders provide texture. Fort-trekking returns mid-month as trails fully dry.
Peak builds at 17-28°C. Karnataka Rajyotsava on November 1. Fort photography delivers year-best granite-and-sky contrast. All surfaces are clean and dry.
Peak season at 15-27°C. All climbing surfaces are at year-clearest. Christmas-New Year rate spike is moderate. Air quality is year-best for fort photography.
January opens peak migrant-bird season at Chorao's Salim Ali sanctuary. 19-30°C is ideal. The free 24-hour Ribandar-Chorao car ferry operates smoothly. Mangrove trails are navigable.
February is the driest month at 20-31°C. Migrant peak holds through mid-February. Carnival traffic in Panaji thins ferry queues briefly. Island pace is peaceful.
March is the last cool window at 22-32°C. Migrant numbers are dropping but still present. Hotel rates ease 20 percent. Quiet beaches and walking trails reward exploration.
Pre-monsoon heat at 25-34°C with 75 percent humidity limits walks to early morning only. The islands' slower pace offers respite from mainland heat.
why_not: Mangrove ecosystems wilt in April's peak heat, limiting wildlife visibility on boat rides and walks.

why_go: Peak heat at 27-36°C with 80 percent humidity. Sanctuary collapses. Pre-monsoon storms arrive in the final 10 days. Hotel rates are year-low.
why_not: Migratory birds have left and temperatures exceed 40°C, making both wildlife visibility and personal comfort scarce.
SW monsoon arrives around June 10 with 700-900mm rain. Sanctuary closes during heavy rain. Ferry delays increase. Mangrove flooding makes exploration miserable.
Heaviest monsoon at 24-29°C brings 800-1,100mm rain. Sanctuary is largely closed. Ferries shut down during peak rains, stranding visitors on islands.

why_go: Monsoon continues at 24-29°C with 600-800mm rain. Bonderam (fourth Saturday of August) on Divar is the year's outlier cultural draw—a Hindu-Muslim shared festival unique to this island.
why_not: August monsoon floods these low-lying islands, making boat access unreliable unless you specifically time your visit around Bonderam Festival.

why_go: Monsoon withdraws at 24-30°C. Rainfall drops to 250-350mm. Sanctuary reopens late month. Islands become walkable again.
why_not: Waterlogged backroads make island exploration tedious in the tail-end monsoon. Early-month conditions remain problematic.

why_go: Season opens at 23-31°C. Post-monsoon green persists with 100-150mm light rain. First migrants arrive mid-month and numbers build toward December.
Peak builds at 21-30°C. Migrant numbers accelerate toward December's peak. Hotel rates climb steadily through the month. Mangrove trails are bone-dry.
Peak season at 19-30°C. Migrant density rivals January levels. Christmas-New Year rates double. The islands offer peace away from beach Goa's chaos.

January opens peak Coimbatore season at 19-30°C. Adiyogi Shiva statue is at clearest visibility from distance. Isha Yoga Center, Marudhamalai, Perur Pateeswarar, and Velliangiri are all easily accessible.
Cool-dry conditions at 20-32°C. Mahashivaratri celebration at Isha (Feb-Mar) features Sadhguru's overnight vigil. Adiyogi statue reaches peak clarity. The plains' pulse is excellent.
Late winter at 21-34°C. If Maha Shivaratri falls in March, Isha is at year-busiest with spiritual seekers. Sightseeing is still excellent early-month.
why_not: Peak heat arrives by late March. Cooler Nilgiris nearby make staying on the plains uncomfortable as April approaches.

why_go: Plains heat dome opens at 23-38°C. Evening operations and early dawn explore the city's cultural sites. Gateway role to Nilgiris remains viable for quick transit.
why_not: April heat peaks at 38°C with dry conditions and minimal rainfall. Daytime sightseeing is uncomfortable.

why_go: Peak heat at 24-39°C compresses sightseeing to dawn-only windows. The spiritual draw of Isha and temples remains, but physical comfort is limited.
why_not: Peak summer heat makes outdoor sightseeing uncomfortable in May. Late-morning and afternoon exploration becomes untenable.

why_go: SW monsoon brings residual 50-100mm rainfall and temperature relief to 23-32°C. Rain-shadow positioning offers advantage over hill stations' monsoon intensity.
why_not: Monsoon rains make outdoor sightseeing unpredictable in June. Activity planning becomes difficult.

why_go: SW monsoon rain-shadow brings 80-150mm rainfall at 23-31°C. City sightseeing is viable. Temperature relief from May is noticeable.
why_not: Monsoon rains peak in July, making outdoor exploration difficult. NH181 and NH183 closures compress the Nilgiri gateway role.

why_go: SW monsoon tails at 23-31°C with 60-120mm rainfall. City sightseeing becomes more workable. Monsoon release has eased the humidity.
why_not: Monsoon rains peak in August, making outdoor exploration uncomfortable and risky. Ghat access remains compromised.

why_go: SW monsoon retreats at 22-31°C. Rainfall eases to 80-150mm. NH181 and NH183 stabilise. Full outdoor itinerary returns. Adiyogi clarity improves.
Year-best window returns at 21-30°C. NE monsoon residual brings 100-180mm rainfall but skies clear afternoon onwards. Adiyogi reaches year-clearest visibility.
why_not: Pre-monsoon humidity and afternoon showers make outdoor sightseeing uncomfortable most days in early October.

why_go: Cool-dry season at 20-29°C. Adiyogi is at year-cleanest. Karthigai Deepam on December 4 is approaching. Rates climb 20 percent through the month.
Peak season at 19-29°C. Christmas-New Year rates climb 25 percent. Nilgiri gateway role is year-busiest. Book accommodations 3-4 weeks ahead.
January opens peak South Goa luxury belt. 18-31°C is ideal. Sea is calm and dry. Margao (7km) is the commercial hub. Hotel-strip fills to capacity.
February is the driest month at 19-31°C. Charter-tourist load eases mid-February. Hotel rates drop 15 percent. Beaches are less crowded than January.
Last cool window at 21-33°C. Charter season ends. Hotel rates drop 25-30 percent. Beaches are peaceful and water is still warm.
Pre-monsoon heat at 24-35°C with 75 percent humidity. Resort pools take centre stage. Early-dawn and dusk beach time is viable.
why_not: April heat peaks above 35°C, limiting beach time to dawn and dusk hours. Midday is untenable.

why_go: Peak heat at 26-37°C with 80 percent humidity. Shacks dismantle May 31. First squalls hit late month, beginning monsoon transformation.
why_not: May brings peak monsoon heat and humidity with few tourists and many closed businesses. The beach experience degrades rapidly.
SW monsoon brings 600-800mm rain and red-flag seas. Shacks shut. Beach becomes dangerous for swimming. Water sports cease entirely.
Peak monsoon at 24-29°C brings 900-1,100mm rain. Beaches are off-limits. Resort occupancy crashes to 20 percent. Rip currents pose serious safety risks.
Monsoon continues at 24-29°C with 700-900mm rain. Beaches are closed, resorts are skeleton crews. Swimming is impossible.

why_go: Monsoon retreats at 25-30°C with 300-400mm rain. Shacks remain closed until October 1. Resort infrastructure rebuilds.
why_not: Beaches remain waterlogged and plagued by seaweed from active monsoon rains. Early-month conditions are worse than late-month.

why_go: Season opens. Shacks reopen October 1 at 23-32°C with 150-200mm rain. Resort rates are 30-35 percent below December. Beaches are clean and walkable.
Peak builds at 20-30°C with rainfall under 30mm. Charter blocks begin arriving. Hotel rates climb 25 percent month-over-month. Beaches are at year-clearest.
Peak season at 18-29°C. Christmas-New Year drives rates 60-80 percent above November. Beaches are full but the South Goa pace remains distinctly local. Book 4 weeks ahead.
January peak opens post-New Year. 8-22°C at 1,850m is crisp. Tea estates are dry and Sim's Park is clear. Nilgiri Mountain Railway's steam-rack section photographs at year-best.
why_not: Heavy frost limits outdoor exploration to midday hours only. Dawn departures are uncomfortable until 9am.

why_go: February is driest with 10-23°C. Tea-estate visibility is cleanest of the year. Mountain air is sharp. Rates drop 20 percent below January.
why_not: Fog hangs thick through most of February, limiting views and outdoor time until late month when clarity improves.

why_go: Cool-dry at 11-25°C. Sim's Park spring flush is at its most colourful. Tea-estate visibility holds steady. This is the last quiet month before April crowds arrive.
Pre-monsoon at 14-27°C. Sim's Park is in full spring flush. Summer-migration spillover from Ooty arrives, but Coonoor stays quieter and more manageable.
Summer-migration spillover at 16-27°C. First fortnight is clean and dry. SW monsoon advance squalls only dominate the final 10 days, leaving a trekking window.
SW monsoon onset at 14-22°C with 200-300mm rainfall. Tea gardens peak in green. Viewpoints become fogged, but the landscape is photogenic.
why_not: Monsoon disrupts toy train schedules frequently. NMR steam section is landslide-affected. Go only if rain-walking is acceptable.
Peak SW monsoon at 14-20°C brings 600-900mm rainfall. Nilgiri Mountain Railway suspends regularly. Viewpoints are unusable. Trails are slippery.
SW monsoon continues at 14-20°C with 400-600mm rainfall. NMR runs reduced schedule. Viewpoints are fogged. Trails are muddy and visibility is poor.

why_go: SW monsoon retreats at 12-22°C with 100-200mm rainfall. Catherine Falls reaches year-peak flow. Tea estates are at greenest. Cool mountain air returns.
Full operations resume at 11-22°C with 100-150mm residual rainfall. Catherine Falls still flows strong. Tea estates remain lush. Mountain clarity begins returning.
Cold-dry at 9-21°C. Tea-estate visibility is year-cleanest. Sim's Park second flush is at its best. Rates climb 25 percent throughout the month.
Peak season at 7-21°C. Christmas-New Year rates double. Sim's Park is year-busiest. The mountain air is crisp and clear. Book 3-4 weeks ahead.
January opens peak coffee-misty season. 13-26°C at 1,170m is ideal. Talakaveri is clear and plantation walks are year-best. Mist and aroma define the experience.
February is driest at 14-28°C. Talakaveri and plantation walks are peak. Misty mornings are frequent. Coffee harvest season is active. Rates remain reasonable.
Coffee Blossom window at 16-30°C. White-blossom carpets blanket plantations 7-10 days after pre-monsoon showers. This is the most fragrant month.
Coffee Blossom tail at 17-31°C. Talakaveri and plantation walks remain workable. Pre-monsoon storms only dominate the final 10 days, leaving a trekking window.
why_not: Pre-monsoon heat and humidity arrive before rains. Trekking becomes uncomfortable despite elevation.

why_go: Pre-monsoon storms at 18-29°C bring spectacular cloud formations. SW monsoon advance squalls only dominate the final 10 days. First-half trekking is viable.
why_not: Pre-monsoon heat and humidity make hiking through coffee plantations exhausting rather than enjoyable.
SW monsoon onset brings 700-900mm rainfall. Landslide risk on NH-275 peaks. The combination of heavy rain and unstable slopes makes travel unsafe.
Peak monsoon at 18-24°C brings 900-1,200mm rainfall. Landslide risk peaks. June-July is coorg's historical vulnerability window for road closures.
SW monsoon continues at 18-25°C with 700-1,000mm rainfall. The 2018 landslide occurred in August. Leeches make every trek a battle, not a walk.

why_go: SW monsoon retreats at 17-26°C with 400-600mm rainfall easing. Plantations reach year-greenest. Abbey Falls flows strong. Cool air returns.
Season opens at 16-26°C. Cauvery Sankramana on October 17. Plantations are year-greenest. Talakaveri is clear and full. The mountain breathes.
High season builds at 14-26°C, dry. Coffee Arabica harvest season begins. Karnataka Rajyotsava on November 1. Plantation walks are impeccable.
Peak season at 12-25°C, dry. Coffee harvest peaks. Huttari Kodava festival marks the Kodava new year. Christmas-New Year rates double.
